recent_posts.content_text:
Hey all, time to close the books on this grant, with iCKB delivered!!
Nothing else changes: iCKB keeps running, I keep working on it and this topic stays open for updates and questions. It’s only the grant that is fully spent.
Here is where the grant went, in short:
Grant: 673,400 CKB, about 10,000 USD at the time.
Refund of the iCKB mainnet deployment and audit: 438,310 CKB.
User and dev support: the other 235,090 CKB, sent to the bot as liquidity. It paid for 35 hours, many more in practice: user updates over the years, the dCKB depositors hunt and investigation, user support here and in Nervos Nation.
As for the projects:

dCKB Rescuer: done too, sadly. Over the years I looked for the original dCKB depositors without success. Then the NervosDAO deposits behind dCKB were drained, so there is nothing left to rescue.
Thank you to everybody who voted, asked questions and tested along the way!! A special thanks to every iCKB user, for trusting iCKB with your CKB
Love & Peace, Phroi

recent_posts.author: SalmanDev
recent_posts.content_text: Thanks, a fork of the cheque lock sounds right. My proposal: (1) the recipient’s claim no longer forces capacity back to the sender, so plain CKB reaches the recipient; (2) the hardcoded 6-epoch delay becomes a per-cell deadline in the args, with the recipient’s claim valid only once an absolute since reaches it; (3) the owner path is always valid, and a heartbeat is the owner recreating the cell with a later deadline (90 days by default in the frontend, any duration allowed). The rest stays as in Cheque. I already have a working version with tests and a full testnet lifecycle in the repo, which I can rebase onto the Cheque source if you prefer. Does this match what you had in mind?

recent_posts.topic_title: [DIS] Cellula on Fiber: a wallet, a checkout and an AI agent on a public mainnet LSP
recent_posts.author: LusoCryptoLabs
recent_posts.content_text:
Fiber works. What it lacks is a way in for people who will never run a node, and Fiber Link, funded by this DAO, says the same. Cellula gives it three: a wallet people open with their face or fingerprint, a checkout any shop adds with two lines, and an agent that lets AI pay for what it uses within limits a person sets. All three pay in seconds over Fiber, and all three already run on testnet. This proposal takes them to mainnet, on a public LSP (the node that opens payment channels for wallets, so they never need one of their own) that any Fiber wallet or app can use.
LusoCryptoLabs asks for $22,258.48 (and up to $1,664 of contingency, paid only if used), in CKB over five payments, each after something anyone can check. The DAO is asked for no liquidity; LusoCryptoLabs puts in the channel capital itself.

How it fits: wallets and agents each hold a channel with the LSP and sign on their own device; shops are paid through invoices the LSP routes; the chain holds the wallet’s scripts and each channel’s opening and close.
Why this matters
People: Fiber Link, funded by this DAO, wrote that “the only obstacle for adoption on Nervos Talk is the absence of a good fiber wallet” (t/9845 #42): a wallet routed through liquidity nodes (#46). This proposal puts that wallet and its liquidity node on mainnet.
Shops: Cellula Checkout lets any site take Fiber payments with two lines, and the money lands on the shop’s own Fiber node.
AI agents: AI and machine payments over Fiber are on the community’s opportunity map for 2026 (t/10665), which lists two LusoCryptoLabs experiments among the pieces to inspect first, Scryve Reads and Trickle; our Cellula agent already makes these payments on testnet, over HTTP 402 and MCP.
A first user on day one: Scryve, the publishing platform LusoCryptoLabs runs in production, already takes instant Fiber tips on testnet, straight to an author’s .cell name. With this LSP on mainnet, its authors get them on mainnet.
The LSP is public: any Fiber wallet or app can use it, not only Cellula. On testnet, LSP2 found a route to the desk of Twine, a P2P CKB desk on Fiber, on 2026-10-31; FiberNuts plans to use a hosted LSP.
The DAO pays for no liquidity and no past work: only the step to mainnet, six months of running it, and help for the projects that use it. The grant is in the range of past grants (Fiber Link $20,000, Invisibook $24,000).
What already works on testnet
Everything this proposal launches runs today on the CKB test network, on LusoCryptoLabs’ public LSP. The grant pays for none of it; it is the evidence. Behind it: five products built since May 2026 at LusoCryptoLabs’ own cost, the .cell names (live on mainnet), the wallet, the Fiber service, Checkout with the agent, and the Android app.

LSP2 runs on Fiber’s LSP support (#1623), which is not merged yet. Until it is, the LSP runs a fork: Fiber’s LSP branch plus LusoCryptoLabs’ fixes, with its source public at github.com/LusoCryptoLabs/fiber, and each fix goes upstream as a pull request. It moves to a Fiber release once one carries what the LSP needs.
What the grant pays for
The grant pays for the work of taking these pieces to mainnet and for six months of running them, nothing already done.

A public status page: wallets, channels, payments routed and opening fees, updated by the LSP itself.
Help for other Fiber projects to use the LSP (Fiber Link, Twine, FiberNuts, or any that asks): its interface documented, and hands-on support.

Six months of operation: monitoring, upgrades as Fiber releases them, and a monthly report on this thread.
It does not pay for past work, channel liquidity, marketing or any token. After month 6 LusoCryptoLabs keeps running the LSP at its own cost, as it runs LSP2 today.

以英文版为准。
Fiber 已经可以使用。它缺少的是一个入口，让那些永远不会自己运行节点的人也能用上它；由本 DAO 资助的 Fiber Link 也这样说。Cellula 提供了三个入口：一个用面容或指纹就能打开的钱包，一个任何商店加两行代码就能接入的收款工具（Checkout），以及一个让 AI 在用户设定的额度内为所用服务付费的代理（agent）。三者都通过 Fiber 在几秒内完成支付，而且都已在测试网上运行。本提案把它们带到主网，运行在一个公共 LSP 上（LSP 是为钱包开通支付通道的节点，钱包因此不需要自己运行节点），任何 Fiber 钱包或应用都可以使用。
LusoCryptoLabs 申请 22,258.48 美元（另有最多 1,664 美元的应急预算，仅在实际使用时支付），以 CKB 分五次支付，每次都在一项任何人都可以核实的交付之后。本提案不向 DAO 申请任何流动性；通道资金由 LusoCryptoLabs 自己投入。
带来什么
（图片见上方英文部分。）
如何组合：钱包和代理各自与 LSP 保持一条通道，并在自己的设备上签名；商店通过 LSP 路由的发票（invoice）收款；链上保存钱包的脚本，以及每条通道的开启和关闭。
为什么重要
个人用户：由本 DAO 资助的 Fiber Link 写道，“在 Nervos Talk 上推广的唯一障碍，是缺少一个好用的 Fiber 钱包”（t/9845 #42），也就是一个通过流动性节点路由的钱包（#46）。本提案正是把这样的钱包及其流动性节点带到主网。
商店：Cellula Checkout 让任何网站加两行代码就能接收 Fiber 付款，钱直接进入商店自己的 Fiber 节点。
AI 代理：通过 Fiber 进行的 AI 和机器支付，已列入社区 2026 年的机会地图（t/10665），地图把 LusoCryptoLabs 的两个实验 Scryve Reads 和 Trickle 列为首先值得查看的项目；我们的 Cellula agent 已经在测试网上通过 HTTP 402 和 MCP 完成这类支付。
第一天就有用户：LusoCryptoLabs 在生产环境中运营的发布平台 Scryve，已经在测试网上接收即时的 Fiber 打赏，直接打到作者的 .cell 名称。这个 LSP 上主网后，作者们就能在主网上收到打赏。
LSP 是公共的：任何 Fiber 钱包或应用都可以使用，不只是 Cellula。2026-10-31，LSP2 在测试网上找到了通往 Twine 交易柜台的路由（Twine 是基于 Fiber 的 P2P CKB 交易柜台）；FiberNuts 计划使用托管 LSP。
DAO 不为流动性付费，也不为过去的工作付费：只为上主网这一步、六个月的运营，以及帮助使用它的项目付费。本资助的金额与以往的资助相当（Fiber Link 20,000 美元，Invisibook 24,000 美元）。
测试网上已经可以使用的部分
本提案要上线的一切，今天都已在 CKB 测试网上运行，运行在 LusoCryptoLabs 的公共 LSP 上。本资助不为其中任何部分付费；它们是证据。其背后是自 2026 年 5 月以来由 LusoCryptoLabs 自费构建的五个产品：.cell 名称（已在主网运行）、钱包、Fiber 服务、带代理的 Checkout，以及 Android 应用。

Fiber works. What it lacks is a way in for people who will never run a node, and Fiber Link, funded by this DAO, says the same. Cellula gives it three: a wallet people open with their face or fingerprint, a checkout any shop adds with two lines, and an agent that lets AI pay for what it uses within limits a person sets. All three pay in seconds over Fiber, and all three already run on testnet. This proposal takes them to mainnet, on a public LSP (the node that opens payment channels for wallets, so they never need one of their own) that any Fiber wallet or app can use.

LusoCryptoLabs asks for $22,258.48 (and up to $1,664 of contingency, paid only if used), in CKB over five payments, each after something anyone can check. The DAO is asked for no liquidity; LusoCryptoLabs puts in the channel capital itself.

How it fits: wallets and agents each hold a channel with the LSP and sign on their own device; shops are paid through invoices the LSP routes; the chain holds the wallet’s scripts and each channel’s opening and close.

Why this matters

  • People: Fiber Link, funded by this DAO, wrote that “the only obstacle for adoption on Nervos Talk is the absence of a good fiber wallet” (t/9845 #42): a wallet routed through liquidity nodes (#46). This proposal puts that wallet and its liquidity node on mainnet.
  • Shops: Cellula Checkout lets any site take Fiber payments with two lines, and the money lands on the shop’s own Fiber node.
  • AI agents: AI and machine payments over Fiber are on the community’s opportunity map for 2026 (t/10665), which lists two LusoCryptoLabs experiments among the pieces to inspect first, Scryve Reads and Trickle; our Cellula agent already makes these payments on testnet, over HTTP 402 and MCP.
  • A first user on day one: Scryve, the publishing platform LusoCryptoLabs runs in production, already takes instant Fiber tips on testnet, straight to an author’s .cell name. With this LSP on mainnet, its authors get them on mainnet.
  • The LSP is public: any Fiber wallet or app can use it, not only Cellula. On testnet, LSP2 found a route to the desk of Twine, a P2P CKB desk on Fiber, on 2026-10-31; FiberNuts plans to use a hosted LSP.
  • The DAO pays for no liquidity and no past work: only the step to mainnet, six months of running it, and help for the projects that use it. The grant is in the range of past grants (Fiber Link $20,000, Invisibook $24,000).

What already works on testnet

Everything this proposal launches runs today on the CKB test network, on LusoCryptoLabs’ public LSP. The grant pays for none of it; it is the evidence. Behind it: five products built since May 2026 at LusoCryptoLabs’ own cost, the .cell names (live on mainnet), the wallet, the Fiber service, Checkout with the agent, and the Android app.

Work on Fiber itself

LusoCryptoLabs works on Fiber itself, and will keep doing so for as long as it runs an LSP. Three fixes are merged upstream (#1703, #1708, #1715) and two more are open (#1718, #1719).

LSP2 runs on Fiber’s LSP support (#1623), which is not merged yet. Until it is, the LSP runs a fork: Fiber’s LSP branch plus LusoCryptoLabs’ fixes, with its source public at github.com/LusoCryptoLabs/fiber, and each fix goes upstream as a pull request. It moves to a Fiber release once one carries what the LSP needs.

What the grant pays for

The grant pays for the work of taking these pieces to mainnet and for six months of running them, nothing already done.

  • Mainnet servers for the LSP, its gateway and a separate guard machine, and their setup; paid for 24 months, and the LSP runs at least that long.
  • Deploying the Cellula wallet’s on-chain scripts on mainnet (LusoCryptoLabs pays the CKB their cells take).
  • Launching the Cellula wallet, Cellula Checkout and the Cellula agent on mainnet, each checked end to end with small amounts.
  • A public status page: wallets, channels, payments routed and opening fees, updated by the LSP itself.
  • Help for other Fiber projects to use the LSP (Fiber Link, Twine, FiberNuts, or any that asks): its interface documented, and hands-on support.
  • Work on Fiber itself: fixes sent upstream as pull requests.
  • Six months of operation: monitoring, upgrades as Fiber releases them, and a monthly report on this thread.

It does not pay for past work, channel liquidity, marketing or any token. After month 6 LusoCryptoLabs keeps running the LSP at its own cost, as it runs LSP2 today.

Fiber 已经可以使用。它缺少的是一个入口，让那些永远不会自己运行节点的人也能用上它；由本 DAO 资助的 Fiber Link 也这样说。Cellula 提供了三个入口：一个用面容或指纹就能打开的钱包，一个任何商店加两行代码就能接入的收款工具（Checkout），以及一个让 AI 在用户设定的额度内为所用服务付费的代理（agent）。三者都通过 Fiber 在几秒内完成支付，而且都已在测试网上运行。本提案把它们带到主网，运行在一个公共 LSP 上（LSP 是为钱包开通支付通道的节点，钱包因此不需要自己运行节点），任何 Fiber 钱包或应用都可以使用。

LusoCryptoLabs 申请 22,258.48 美元（另有最多 1,664 美元的应急预算，仅在实际使用时支付），以 CKB 分五次支付，每次都在一项任何人都可以核实的交付之后。本提案不向 DAO 申请任何流动性；通道资金由 LusoCryptoLabs 自己投入。

带来什么

（图片见上方英文部分。）

如何组合：钱包和代理各自与 LSP 保持一条通道，并在自己的设备上签名；商店通过 LSP 路由的发票（invoice）收款；链上保存钱包的脚本，以及每条通道的开启和关闭。

为什么重要

  • 个人用户：由本 DAO 资助的 Fiber Link 写道，“在 Nervos Talk 上推广的唯一障碍，是缺少一个好用的 Fiber 钱包”（t/9845 #42），也就是一个通过流动性节点路由的钱包（#46）。本提案正是把这样的钱包及其流动性节点带到主网。
  • 商店：Cellula Checkout 让任何网站加两行代码就能接收 Fiber 付款，钱直接进入商店自己的 Fiber 节点。
  • AI 代理：通过 Fiber 进行的 AI 和机器支付，已列入社区 2026 年的机会地图（t/10665），地图把 LusoCryptoLabs 的两个实验 Scryve Reads 和 Trickle 列为首先值得查看的项目；我们的 Cellula agent 已经在测试网上通过 HTTP 402 和 MCP 完成这类支付。
  • 第一天就有用户：LusoCryptoLabs 在生产环境中运营的发布平台 Scryve，已经在测试网上接收即时的 Fiber 打赏，直接打到作者的 .cell 名称。这个 LSP 上主网后，作者们就能在主网上收到打赏。
  • LSP 是公共的：任何 Fiber 钱包或应用都可以使用，不只是 Cellula。2026-10-31，LSP2 在测试网上找到了通往 Twine 交易柜台的路由（Twine 是基于 Fiber 的 P2P CKB 交易柜台）；FiberNuts 计划使用托管 LSP。
  • DAO 不为流动性付费，也不为过去的工作付费：只为上主网这一步、六个月的运营，以及帮助使用它的项目付费。本资助的金额与以往的资助相当（Fiber Link 20,000 美元，Invisibook 24,000 美元）。

测试网上已经可以使用的部分

本提案要上线的一切，今天都已在 CKB 测试网上运行，运行在 LusoCryptoLabs 的公共 LSP 上。本资助不为其中任何部分付费；它们是证据。其背后是自 2026 年 5 月以来由 LusoCryptoLabs 自费构建的五个产品：.cell 名称（已在主网运行）、钱包、Fiber 服务、带代理的 Checkout，以及 Android 应用。

本资助支付把这些组件带到主网的工作，以及六个月的运营，不支付任何已完成的工作。

  • 在主网部署 Cellula 钱包的链上脚本（脚本所占 cell 的 CKB 由 LusoCryptoLabs 支付）。
  • 在主网上线 Cellula 钱包、Cellula Checkout 和 Cellula agent，每一项都用小额资金做端到端检查。
  • 一个公开的状态页面：钱包、通道、路由的付款和开通费用，由 LSP 自己更新。

  • 六个月的运营：监控、随 Fiber 新版本升级，并每月在本帖发布报告。

本资助不支付过去的工作、通道流动性、市场推广或任何代币。第 6 个月之后，LusoCryptoLabs 将自费继续运行这个 LSP，就像今天运行 LSP2 一样。

风险

DAO 按里程碑付款，且不持有任何资金，因此一次失败最多让它损失下一笔付款。

风险 应对
拿到 LSP 密钥的人可以动用通道资金 在主网持有资金之前，决定密钥如何保管并写在本帖；涉及的资金属于 LusoCryptoLabs，而不是 DAO

LSP 停止运行 LusoCryptoLabs 是一个工作室，有多人参与这些产品。即使 LSP 停止运行，每个钱包都在自己的设备上签名，余额仍属于自己：关闭通道即可在链上取回。
会有人用吗？ Cellula 为 Fiber 带来一个完整的钱包（见"为什么重要"），而且 LSP 向任何其他钱包或应用开放。月度报告会公布由 LSP 自己统计的钱包、通道和付款数据。
涉及真实资金的故障 每个里程碑都先用小额资金检查；代理在主网上保留其支出额度

LusoCryptoLabs 是一家位于葡萄牙的软件工作室。它在主网上运营 .cell 名称，并在测试网上构建和运营 LSP2、Cellula 钱包、Cellula Checkout 和 Cellula agent；上面提到的 Fiber 修复由它提交，它还运营 CKB Pulse，一个实时展示谁在 CKB 上构建的页面。

topics.title: Introducing CKB Cell Framework: typed Cells and declarative validation in Rust

recent_posts.topic_title: Introducing CKB Cell Framework: typed Cells and declarative validation in Rust
recent_posts.author: asondev
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi everyone,
We’d like to introduce CKB Cell Framework, a Rust framework for building CKB contracts, developed by FoundationLab.
Our goal is to make CKB contracts easier to write, understand, and test. The framework brings together typed Cell loading, declarative constraints, automatic serialization, transaction construction, and local VM testing.
The main building blocks are:
CellCodec generates encoding, strict decoding, and wire-format schemas for application data.
Cells declares the inputs, outputs, and dependencies an operation needs, with constraints for scripts, capacity, positions, and data.
Context<C> gives handlers access to the loaded Cell collection and executing Script.
StateTransition defines pure transition logic that contracts, clients, and tests can share.
For example, a Counter update declares the relationship between its input and output Cells:
#[derive(Cells)]
#[cells(args = CounterArgs)]
pub struct Update {
#[cell(
source = Source::Input,
type_script = Some(&args.script),
capacity = STATE_CAPACITY,
constraint =
script::script_hash(before.lock()) == before.data().owner
)]
pub before: Cell<State>,
#[cell(
source = Source::Output,
type_script = Some(&args.script),
lock = before.lock(),
capacity = STATE_CAPACITY
)]
pub after: Cell<State>,
}
The handler receives Context<Update> and explicitly validates the expected state transition and actor authorization. Asset contracts additionally verify reserve provenance, supply changes, and actual net payments.
This separation keeps field loading concise while making the remaining protocol checks visible in ordinary Rust functions. Clients construct the proposed transaction; contracts validate its inputs, outputs, and witnesses.
The framework includes unsigned transaction builders for single and multiple reserves, helpers that bind Action witnesses to the actual State input, CKB-VM testing utilities, and schema/IDL export facilities.
Six examples demonstrate the current APIs:
Counter: creation, updates, and owner authorization.
Vault: deposits, withdrawals, and capacity refunds.
Escrow: two-party payment release and refunds.
Vesting: scheduled claims bound to the State input’s since.
Limit Order: partial fills, exact payments, and integer rounding.
AMM: two reserves, liquidity operations, constant-product swaps, and official xUDT LP tokens.
Workspace commands cover project generation, builds, tests, and registered interface exports:
cargo cell new my-contract
cargo check -p my-contract-script
cargo cell build my-contract-script
cargo cell test
We’d welcome feedback from the community, especially on API ergonomics, validation clarity, and patterns needed for real applications.
Repository and documentation: github.com/ckbswap/ckb-cell-framework

topics.title: Same lock script in Rust and in ckb-js-vm: 15k cycles vs 15M

recent_posts.topic_title: Same lock script in Rust and in ckb-js-vm: 15k cycles vs 15M
recent_posts.author: tun_tunn03
recent_posts.content_text:
I wrote the same CKB lock script twice, once in Rust and once in TypeScript for ckb-js-vm, and ran both through the same 58 scenarios in the real CKB-VM. They agree on every accept/reject decision. The cost is very different, and most of the difference is not where I expected.
The script is the session lock from ckb-session-kit. It lets a browser-held session key spend a bounded amount (per-transaction limit, optional single recipient, optional rate limit, no splitting of session cells, no type scripts the key could use to freeze funds), while the owner can always sweep. It also has a token mode that bounds xUDT amounts the same way. It delegates signature checks to the standard locks, so it does no cryptography. That makes it a test of the VM rather than of a crypto library.
Results (the lock’s own script group only):
Rust ckb-js-vm
Code deployed 7,656 B 30,917 B bytecode + 410,248 B VM
Mean cycles, accepted CKB spends 14,758 15,037,968
Mean cycles, accepted token spends 20,348 15,518,698
Median ratio, all 58 scenarios 1x 1009x
Cheapest run (args rejected) 3,145 14,272,805
What surprised me: the cheapest ckb-js-vm run, which rejects the args almost immediately, still costs 14.3M cycles. That is starting the JavaScript VM and loading the bytecode. An accepted spend costs 15.04M, so the lock’s own logic is about 0.77M cycles, around 5% of the total. The logic runs at roughly 66x the Rust logic’s cycles, but for a script this small the fixed start-up cost dominates.
For scale, a standard secp256k1 lock costs about 1.6M cycles. So the Rust session lock adds under 1% to a typical spend, and the ckb-js-vm version adds about 9x a signature check.
The lock gained three rules and a token mode after my first measurement on 8 Oct, so I re-ran the original 20 scenarios against both versions. The Rust lock’s accepted spends went from 12,263 to 15,393 cycles (+26%: a bigger binary and checks on every output). The ckb-js-vm version went from 14.57M to 15.07M (+3%), and most of that was start-up again. The 8 Oct TypeScript port, rebuilt today, still costs exactly its 8 Oct cycles, so the extra 0.36M comes from loading 1.8 KB more bytecode.
What I take from it:
For small, frequently run scripts like locks, ckb-js-vm’s start-up cost is the number to know. It does not shrink with better JavaScript, and it grows with bytecode size.
For larger or rarely run scripts, or for prototyping, ckb-js-vm is a real option. The TypeScript version was much faster to write, and the logic overhead (66x) is smaller than the headline ratio (about 1000x) suggests.
Writing it twice doubles as a test. Two independent implementations must agree on all 58 scenarios, in CI. Porting the new rules to TypeScript was a useful second read of the Rust code.
How it is measured: ckb-cycle-tools runs each scenario in ckb-debugger through ckb-testtool, one run per script group. CI rebuilds both implementations from source, the Rust lock from a pinned session-kit commit, and re-runs every scenario, so the numbers are reproducible from a clean checkout. Five of the ckb-js-vm scenarios are also in a cross-version check: every ckb-debugger release from 0.121.0 to 1.1.1, native and WebAssembly (14 builds), gave the same cycles and the same result.
The same tool works on your own contracts. Since ckb-cycle-tools 1.1.0 (npm, 31 Oct), a project made from ckb-script-templates can use its existing ckb-testtool tests as the scenarios: a helper call saves each test’s transaction, ckb-cycles scan writes the config, and ckb-cycles report gives cycles per script group and the costliest functions. Steps are in the README.

topics.title: iCKB is now fully on CCC: new DApp, SDK and Bot

recent_posts.topic_title: iCKB is now fully on CCC: new DApp, SDK and Bot
recent_posts.author: phroi
recent_posts.content_text:
Hey all
Last month I promised good news on the iCKB side: here it is!! ickb.org now runs a brand new DApp, built together with a new SDK and a new bot, all on CCC
They replace the Lumos versions that served iCKB since 2024: the old DApp, the old bot and their libraries @ickb/v1-core and @ickb/lumos-utils. Lumos is no longer actively maintained, so the move was overdue. Now it’s done!!
In June I wrote about a setback with CCC UDT support. That setback is behind us: the SDK doesn’t need it at all, it reads iCKB cells with CCC core alone.
Safety first
The new code runs on the same contracts, so I went back to them too. They can’t be changed on chain, so I tried hard to make them accept something they shouldn’t: almost 50 million attempts, each checked against the four protocol rules. They held every single time, not a single break!! Anyone can also rebuild them from source and get exactly the bytes running on chain. All the details are in iCKB Contracts Revisited and its report.
The new stack adds its own guard: the DApp reads the chain through public nodes, so now the SDK checks what a node says before your wallet signs. Each cell is checked against the transaction that created it, each header against its hash.
Users
The DApp before connecting a wallet1536×2084 187 KB
Look before you connect: the DApp quotes a conversion and shows what your CKB is worth in iCKB over time, with no wallet connected. The old DApp asked for JoyID first.
The wallet list1536×2084 218 KB
Any wallet CCC supports: JoyID and UTXO Global, but also MetaMask, OKX, UniSat and other EVM, Bitcoin or Nostr wallets, or a wallet on another device through Khie pairing. The old DApp supported JoyID only.
A conversion preview, before signing1902×2579 336 KB
Know before you sign: the preview is the real transaction, rebuilt once more right before your wallet pops up. Under the button the DApp says in plain words what it does:
a direct conversion, at a fixed time;
an order, converted when a bot fills it;
or part of each.
An order also says how much CKB it holds as cell space, returned when you collect. Then the DApp shows one Ready date for everything you have converting, plus the fee.
All your CKB: the old DApp held back 600 CKB from every conversion. Now you can convert what you have. If it’s not enough for fees and cells, the DApp tells you before signing.
Deposits spread over the whole DAO cycle: the bot now actively spreads pool deposits along the roughly 30 days of a NervosDAO cycle, instead of leaving them lumped together. In the February 2025 liquidity crunch the closest deposit ended up two weeks away. Spreading takes one cycle to settle, so withdrawal times should improve considerably once this first month passes.
Faster fills: orders now pay bots a 0.01% fee instead of 0.001%. At 0.001%, DAO growth put a CKB to iCKB order under par within four hours, so no bot would touch it. At 0.01% an order stays worth filling for about two days.
Converted funds ready to collect1902×2579 286 KB
That 2,000 CKB order was filled by the testnet bot about five minutes after it committed.
Collecting is part of every transaction: each transaction you sign also collects what is ready. To only collect, leave the amount at zero.
Orders don’t get stuck: an order older than thirty days comes back to you with your next transaction. A buy that bots refuse to fill also comes back.
Small amounts: a few iCKB can often still go back to CKB, which also frees the CKB behind a small iCKB cell.
Send everything elsewhere: point the address in the header to another wallet and the next transaction sends your CKB and iCKB there. That’s the way out for a wallet that can’t transfer xUDT tokens itself.
Integrators
Install @ickb/sdk: one package, whose only dependency is CCC itself (@ckb-ccc/core, as a peer). It works in the browser too.
The Lumos libraries were two packages pulling in eight Lumos packages. The new flow follows CCC:
IckbSdk.fromChain(chain);
getL1AccountState(...) reads the account, the pool and the order book;
buildConversionTransaction(...) returns a funded transaction with its planned fee;
signAndSendTransaction(...), then waitTransaction(...).
The SDK README explains each step and the reasons behind it.
Operators
The bot is now one process running a turn every ten minutes:
the signing key lives in a 0600 file, not in an environment variable;
each turn writes JSON lines to the journal, including why it did nothing, so you can tell a quiet market from an empty wallet;
on any error it exits and systemd restarts it clean.
It has been running on testnet since September. The bot README covers setup and the journal.
Try it
Open ickb.org, pick Testnet and grab some CKB from the faucet link under CKB. The screenshots above are from testnet.
Everything is in one repository: ickb/stack. Feedback is very welcome, here or in the Nervos Nation iCKB channel.
Love & Peace,
Phroi

recent_posts.topic_title: iCKB Contracts Revisited: Old Code, New Audit
recent_posts.author: phroi
recent_posts.content_text:
Hey all~ @ArthurZhang, glad the scenario map helped!
iCKB safety has always been my priority. With all the recent LLM incidents, I went back to the contracts. I was already pretty sure there was no issue (but you never know), so I threw at them every technique I could think of, fuzzing first and foremost!!
Right now, the greater concern I have is over the continuous reporting of vulnerabilities and breaches: PHP, Node.js, Binance, even the Linux kernel itself, all in ten days of October.
The time correlation is pretty telling: AI is what enables the speed of these developments, on both sides.
So once again I put that same speed on our side: I just want to be sure we’re doing our best to keep the contracts as safe as possible. They can’t be changed on chain, so I tried hard to make them accept something they shouldn’t. They held every single time!!
Same bytes: anyone can rebuild the contracts from source and get exactly the bytes running on chain.
Millions of attempts: 12 million random transactions plus every small combination of tricky cells (37.8 million more), each checked against the four protocol rules: over 50 hours of computing. Not a single break.
Real network rules: the tests now apply the same checks a CKB node runs. Every real iCKB transaction so far passes them.
Testing the tests: of the 231 planted bugs that still compiled, the tests catch 229. The other two change nothing.
A lying node can’t steal: since stack#66, the iCKB SDK checks what a node says before signing. A lying node can only make a transaction fail.
Bottom line: the iCKB contracts hold up, with nothing new found!! The one known limitation is still the fake limit order trick, which the iCKB Stack guards against. The report has the details and how to repeat every check. The appendix still maps every scenario to the section that traces it.
Love & Peace,
Phroi

topics.title: Myelin Is in Production — Where Could It Take Us Next?

recent_posts.topic_title: Myelin Is in Production — Where Could It Take Us Next?
recent_posts.author: ArthurZhang
recent_posts.content_text:
For anyone new to the project, Myelin is an off-chain runtime I’m building around CKB’s Cell model. It handles application state changes and keeps a history that can be replayed and checked. A session might cover a match, a dungeon run or a stretch of activity in a persistent world. I started it to explore how applications could make use of CKB’s approach to state and verification without sending every interaction to the blockchain.
Myelin is now running in production behind games on UTXOPlay. I’m rather pleased to finally be able to write that.
The 26 October deployment succssfully separated the store from eight game services covering thirteen curated games. Each service now keeps its own rules, runtime and saved states. It is very satisfying to see chess, arcade games and multiplayer matches like Nightshift and BotStrike have given Myelin something considerably more challenging and fun to work with than test fixtures.
In the original Myelin discussion, I wanted to explore how far CKB’s Cell model could travel beyond on-chain execution. The later post on continuous operation took that into longer-running applications, with bounded batches, durable checkpoints and pluggable chain modules.
Games have since given me a slightly different reason to keep building it.
I expect UTXOPlay to attract more games built by one person or a handful of contributors. Some may grow well beyond their original plans. Others might be fun for a fortnight and then disappear.
image1672×941 358 KB
I’d like even the short-lived ones to leave something behind. If somebody picks up an old game a year later, why should its players have to lose every achievement just because the original server is gone?
A small project shouldn’t have to become a permanent company before its players can build something lasting around it either. That possibility is becoming one of my reasons for working on Myelin.
Where Cells become useful
On the CellTx execution path, Myelin’s CellDAG builds an execution plan from transaction dependencies and declared logical read/write accesses. Two transactions trying to consume the same input OutPoint cannot both be accepted. Different Cells can also belong to the same logical conflict domain: reads may coexist, but an access involving a write may require ordering. Myelin resolves those domains from authenticated Cell state, rather than trusting an arbitrary key supplied by the transaction builder.
1536×1024 277 KB
The application still has to choose a sensible state layout.
Put an entire RPG world in one Cell, and two players chopping trees at opposite ends of the map will compete for the same input. The scheduler cannot make that conflict disappear. Split the world into smaller pieces, and more work can proceed independently, at the cost of coordinating operations that cross those boundaries.
That is a useful design problem. Two unrelated matches should be able to progress independently. Two players spending the same unique item should not. The state layout ought to express the difference.
Not every game event needs to become a Cell transaction, either. Movement, animation and client-side prediction belong in the game engine. Myelin has native replay integrations as well as its strict CellTx/CKB-VM path, so an application can choose which parts of its execution need which treatment.
Consider a forest in an RPG. Its server can decide that a tree has fallen. If the resulting timber is later sold into another game’s economy, somebody else now has a reason to care how it was created and who may spend it.
That is a useful place to draw a verification boundary. I want applications to keep their own pace while making the claims they pass to others precise enough to inspect.
For me, that is where the connection back to CKB becomes especially interesting. A game needn’t put its whole simulation on-chain to make selected assets, commitments and outcomes enforceable.
What could travel between games?
I’ve been separating the cross-session work into three operations.
image1536×1024 240 KB
Continuation closes a session and establishes an authorised successor. The successor carries forward the accepted state, or applies an explicitly defined migration when the rules or state format change.
Handoff moves a particular object or right between sessions. For an exclusive right, the source and destination need to agree on its disposition so that transferring it doesn’t leave two independently usable copies.
Stitching combines evidence from separate histories. A tournament could verify results from three different games and calculate an overall result without making those games share a database or a consensus group.
These distinctions are being worked through in #7.
Myelin already has foundations for successors and shared-store handoffs. The next step is to make those operations work across independently operated services.
That adds some quite specific problems. Suppose a destination consumes a transfer but its acknowledgement never reaches the source. The source cannot safely release the item again just because a timer expires. The protocol needs a recoverable way to establish whether consumption or cancellation became final. That is the work in #16 and #17.
Stitching gives us an earlier opportunity to do something useful. A game result can contribute to a tournament, an achievement or a player’s history without transferring an exclusive asset. The receiving application decides which rules and authorities it recognises, then checks the records under those assumptions.
I rather like the idea that the same item could mean different things in different games.
A sword earned in one might qualify its holder for a tournament in another. The second game needn’t inherit the first game’s combat system. It needs to decide whether it accepts the item’s history, how it checks ownership, and what that combination means locally.
Players could carry something of their earlier adventures with them, while developers remain free to invent quite different worlds.
This is also why I’m interested in Spore as a persistent asset identity alongside separately governed game state. The identity can remain recognisable while individual games interpret it through their own rules.
image1536×1024 226 KB
I don’t particularly want every game to agree on what a sword should do. I’d much rather give developers a way to recognise where it came from and decide for themselves.
A world that can change without losing its past
A long-lived world will eventually change its code, its operators and probably some of its rules.
I’d like a player to return after all that and still be able to follow what happened to their character. A balance update might change a sword’s abilities; it should not quietly change the record of how the sword was earned.
Successor sessions give those changes an explicit place in the history. That is the kind of continuity I want to preserve.
It’s one reason I want to return to the Veloren integration. The experiment kept movement, rendering and physics in the ordinary game loop, while selected persistent events entered a journal and were processed in bounded CellTx batches.
For example, a client may predict that a shot hit before the authoritative simulation has resolved it. The adapter needs to know when the result is settled enough to become a persistent reward or inventory change. Recording the speculative result too early would preserve the wrong decision very reliably.
The same care is needed around simulation ticks, randomness and engine versions. I want reusable adapters to make these choices explicit without forcing every developer to write the integration from scratch. That is #19.
For persistent RPGs, I’d like to explore sessions corresponding to actual lifecycles: a dungeon run, a regional history, a player inventory or a season. Some would finish quickly; others would advance through many epochs.
A dungeon could close while the characters who entered it continue elsewhere. A season could end without erasing the world that hosted it. A regional service could move to another operator without everyone having to abandon their progress.
The bounded-session model starts to look useful in its own right here. It gives a change of rules or responsibility a definite place to happen.
The practical work is in successor compatibility and migration, portable historical evidence, and archival and recovery.
I’d be delighted to see a world survive several changes of implementation and still feel, to its players, like the place they helped build.
When a game grows beyond its maker
image1774×887 297 KB
Myelin’s chain-module work has a similar purpose.
The continuous-operation post described the separation between production, execution, finality, networking and storage. My simultaneous work back then introduced an optional, vendor-customisable L2 chain-module, with finality options including proof of authority, a static committee and Tendermint-style agreement among known validators.
A centrally operated browser game can use a single authority. Several independent operators might prefer a committee or a multi-round agreement protocol. The execution layer still checks the transitions; the chosen finality module determines how the configured operators accept the resulting block.
I’m less interested in making every game select a sophisticated consensus system than in giving it somewhere to go when its circumstances change.
Suppose a community eventually wants to run a game I began on my own. I’d like there to be a straightforward way to hand it over without asking everyone to forget its earlier history.
A successor could record the last accepted state, the new operators and any agreed changes to the rules. Earlier matches would still be checked under the rules they were played under.
That would give a small project a way to grow beyond its original operator.
Finality configuration is bound to session genesis, so this would be an explicit transition rather than a module quietly being replaced halfway through a history. State conversions, outstanding commands and uncompleted transfers would have to be accounted for during the move.
This is the application-chain direction I want to explore: an application operating its own durable session history, with room to change its rules and organisation through recorded transitions.
The participants would still decide which continuation they wanted to follow. What I can build is a way for them to inspect what was carried over and what changed.
That seems more useful than requiring a small game to settle every question about its eventual governance before anyone has played it.
Different applications, different clocks
The IoT idea from the original discussion has stayed with me. I keep wondering what happens to a machine’s history when the company running its software disappears. Imagine a pump still working twenty years after its manufacturer has gone out of business. The people maintaining it might have its service records, its usage history and several generations of replacement parts. I would like its digital history to be something they can inherit and understand too.
image1535×1024 249 KB
There is a more immediate experiment I’d like to try. Imagine a small energy co-operative: a few homes, a workshop, some solar panels and a shared battery. During the day, each carries on with its own work. By evening, the members need to agree how much energy was supplied, how it was used and what each participant owes. A disagreement over the bill should be something they can investigate themselves.
The IoT profile in Myelin’s positioning document starts with devices signing readings and an edge gateway collecting them into batches. Each batch would carry a commitment to the readings and the rule used to aggregate them. Myelin would check the signatures and calculations, then record the resulting state change. There would be no reason to create a Cell for every flicker of a sensor. A useful session might cover a billing period, a production shift or a particular service agreement. The proposed CKB court path would give a disputed batch somewhere to be checked against its settlement rules.
What interests me is how far that arrangement could extend beyond one operator. The workshop might change its electricity supplier. The co-operative might replace its gateway or bring in a different company to maintain the battery. I’d like those changes to be possible without surrendering the accounts to whoever happens to run the next dashboard. Earlier obligations would still need to be understood under the agreements that created them.
Further out, I can imagine software agents arranging these short service sessions on behalf of machines. A delivery robot could negotiate a charging stop within a budget its owner had authorised. The charger and the robot would produce receipts for the service, settle the agreed charge and go their separate ways. Neither owner would need to join a platform governing everything the other machine does. They would need an agreement precise enough to check, recognised identities and a way to deal with a failed or disputed exchange.
That starts to suggest a rather different way of organising connected infrastructure. Equipment could participate in temporary arrangements, leave them, and carry the relevant records into the next one. A small operator could offer a service without first persuading every customer to adopt its entire software system. I’d be curious to see what people build when cooperation can begin with one modest, inspectable agreement.
The work through Q1 2027
The current work is collected in Myelin #6. I’m aiming to finish this roadmap and the associated UTXOPlay integration issues by the end of Q1 2027.
Area
Issues
Cross-session rules and resource limits
#7 — Protocol definitions, #8 — Handoff regression tests, #9 — Aggregate resource budgets, #10 — Application authorisation
Continuity, recovery and migration
#11 — Shared-store transfer and cancellation, #12 — Durable command recovery, #14 — Successor compatibility, #15 — Writer fencing, #18 — Archival and recovery budgets
Portable evidence and independent services
#13 — Evidence bundles and historical replayers, #16 — Remote proofs and inboxes, #17 — Transfer outcomes and refunds
Game integration and measurements
#19 — Reusable application adapters, #20 — Real-workload benchmarks, #21 — Reproducible acceptance tests
CKB enforcement
#22 — Game-to-CKB testnet dispute and exit example
I also want proper measurements across native and CKB-VM workloads: commit latency, memory use, recovery time and the effect of running several sessions together. Those should help developers choose a configuration for their game, rather than inherit one from an unrelated example.
The CKB reference path in #22 starts with a small game whose disputed transition can actually be checked by a CKB script. The aim is a reproducible opening, execution, challenge and exit flow that other applications can learn from.
UTXOPlay has its own companion issues:
Issue
Work
UTXOPlay #2
Rebuildable Session Registry and evidence index
UTXOPlay #3
Independently verified leaderboards and cross-game achievements
UTXOPlay #4
Command recovery integration while preserving historical saves
UTXOPlay #5
Read-only Spore/DOB cosmetic entitlements
UTXOPlay #6
Verified game results feeding testnet achievement issuance
I’m particularly looking forward to the point where someone can take an old session, obtain the exact rules it used, and reproduce its result on a clean machine.
That gives another developer something they can choose to recognise in their own application. They might build a tournament around it, continue the original game, or give an old achievement an entirely unexpected use.
I’d like to leave that choice open.
Come and build something
image1536×1024 176 KB
So far, I’ve been the only person designing and building Myelin. Now UTXOPlay has given us somewhere to try these ideas, and I’d love to see people build games I would never have thought of.
There’s much room to work on the session runtime, make something for UTXOPlay, or try the model in other types of applications. A random arcade game or an awkward integration would be a very welcome place to start.
Send me a DM if any of this gives you an idea.

Suppose a community eventually wants to run a game I began on my own. I’d like there to be a straightforward way to hand it over without asking everyone to forget its earlier history.

A successor could record the last accepted state, the new operators and any agreed changes to the rules. Earlier matches would still be checked under the rules they were played under.

That would give a small project a way to grow beyond its original operator.

Finality configuration is bound to session genesis, so this would be an explicit transition rather than a module quietly being replaced halfway through a history. State conversions, outstanding commands and uncompleted transfers would have to be accounted for during the move.

This is the application-chain direction I want to explore: an application operating its own durable session history, with room to change its rules and organisation through recorded transitions.

The participants would still decide which continuation they wanted to follow. What I can build is a way for them to inspect what was carried over and what changed.

That seems more useful than requiring a small game to settle every question about its eventual governance before anyone has played it.

Different applications, different clocks

The IoT idea from the original discussion has stayed with me. I keep wondering what happens to a machine’s history when the company running its software disappears. Imagine a pump still working twenty years after its manufacturer has gone out of business. The people maintaining it might have its service records, its usage history and several generations of replacement parts. I would like its digital history to be something they can inherit and understand too.

image1535×1024 249 KB

There is a more immediate experiment I’d like to try. Imagine a small energy co-operative: a few homes, a workshop, some solar panels and a shared battery. During the day, each carries on with its own work. By evening, the members need to agree how much energy was supplied, how it was used and what each participant owes. A disagreement over the bill should be something they can investigate themselves.

The IoT profile in Myelin’s positioning document starts with devices signing readings and an edge gateway collecting them into batches. Each batch would carry a commitment to the readings and the rule used to aggregate them. Myelin would check the signatures and calculations, then record the resulting state change. There would be no reason to create a Cell for every flicker of a sensor. A useful session might cover a billing period, a production shift or a particular service agreement. The proposed CKB court path would give a disputed batch somewhere to be checked against its settlement rules.

What interests me is how far that arrangement could extend beyond one operator. The workshop might change its electricity supplier. The co-operative might replace its gateway or bring in a different company to maintain the battery. I’d like those changes to be possible without surrendering the accounts to whoever happens to run the next dashboard. Earlier obligations would still need to be understood under the agreements that created them.

Further out, I can imagine software agents arranging these short service sessions on behalf of machines. A delivery robot could negotiate a charging stop within a budget its owner had authorised. The charger and the robot would produce receipts for the service, settle the agreed charge and go their separate ways. Neither owner would need to join a platform governing everything the other machine does. They would need an agreement precise enough to check, recognised identities and a way to deal with a failed or disputed exchange.

That starts to suggest a rather different way of organising connected infrastructure. Equipment could participate in temporary arrangements, leave them, and carry the relevant records into the next one. A small operator could offer a service without first persuading every customer to adopt its entire software system. I’d be curious to see what people build when cooperation can begin with one modest, inspectable agreement.

The work through Q1 2027

The current work is collected in Myelin #6. I’m aiming to finish this roadmap and the associated UTXOPlay integration issues by the end of Q1 2027.

Area Issues
Cross-session rules and resource limits #7 — Protocol definitions, #8 — Handoff regression tests, #9 — Aggregate resource budgets, #10 — Application authorisation
Continuity, recovery and migration #11 — Shared-store transfer and cancellation, #12 — Durable command recovery, #14 — Successor compatibility, #15 — Writer fencing, #18 — Archival and recovery budgets
Portable evidence and independent services #13 — Evidence bundles and historical replayers, #16 — Remote proofs and inboxes, #17 — Transfer outcomes and refunds
Game integration and measurements #19 — Reusable application adapters, #20 — Real-workload benchmarks, #21 — Reproducible acceptance tests
CKB enforcement #22 — Game-to-CKB testnet dispute and exit example

I also want proper measurements across native and CKB-VM workloads: commit latency, memory use, recovery time and the effect of running several sessions together. Those should help developers choose a configuration for their game, rather than inherit one from an unrelated example.

The CKB reference path in #22 starts with a small game whose disputed transition can actually be checked by a CKB script. The aim is a reproducible opening, execution, challenge and exit flow that other applications can learn from.

UTXOPlay has its own companion issues:

Issue Work
UTXOPlay #2 Rebuildable Session Registry and evidence index
UTXOPlay #3 Independently verified leaderboards and cross-game achievements
UTXOPlay #4 Command recovery integration while preserving historical saves
UTXOPlay #5 Read-only Spore/DOB cosmetic entitlements
UTXOPlay #6 Verified game results feeding testnet achievement issuance

I’m particularly looking forward to the point where someone can take an old session, obtain the exact rules it used, and reproduce its result on a clean machine.

That gives another developer something they can choose to recognise in their own application. They might build a tournament around it, continue the original game, or give an old achievement an entirely unexpected use.

I’d like to leave that choice open.

Come and build something

image1536×1024 176 KB

So far, I’ve been the only person designing and building Myelin. Now UTXOPlay has given us somewhere to try these ideas, and I’d love to see people build games I would never have thought of.

There’s much room to work on the session runtime, make something for UTXOPlay, or try the model in other types of applications. A random arcade game or an awkward integration would be a very welcome place to start.

Send me a DM if any of this gives you an idea.

recent_posts.author: Code3ks
recent_posts.content_text:
Thanks for the review, and especially for offering to open an RUSD channel to the testnet mint. That would be helpful for interoperability testing.
1. Hosted LSP: I will operate the hosted LSP as a grant deliverable, allowing users to open and manage Fiber channels without running their own FNN node. Users provide their own on-chain RUSD and required CKB capacity, while retaining the client signing role. Applicable mint, LSP and routing fees will be disclosed before approval. I’ll also test interoperability with Fiber’s hosted LSP when available.
2. Onboarding: Users connect a supported CKB wallet to the FiberNuts browser wallet, review and approve the RUSD funding, CKB capacity and fees, then wait for their hosted channel to become ready. They can subsequently fund their Cashu wallet through Fiber and receive proofs after settlement. This is public-testnet onboarding, not a free funding service.
3. Milestones and mainnet: The $6,000 grant is divided into four $1,500 payments: at project start and after accepted reports at weeks 4, 8 and 12. Deliverables progress from settlement reliability and recovery to hosted-LSP onboarding, followed by the versioned package, independent deployment, reliability testing and Community Market pilot. Reviewers receive at least seven days per report.
Mainnet is limited to an operator-funded, gated direct-channel validation: 10 reconciled operations, maximum 5 RUSD per operation and 50 RUSD total live liability. It proceeds only if the verification, testnet and incident-plan requirements are met. No public mainnet mint or LSP is included.
The testnet mint is live at https://mint.fibernuts.xyz.
I will ping you when it’s about time. Thanks
